text: Course five's GlideRecord performance pitfalls lesson already covered this: querying inside a loop, skipping setLimit, looping through records just to count them. This lesson is about seeing those mistakes once you're actually measuring a transaction, instead of reading code line by line.

A query that runs once outside a loop shows up in the debug panel as exactly one line. A query that got left inside a loop shows up as the same query, repeated — the profiler can roll it up into one line with an execution count attached, something like a problem query appearing forty-seven times in one transaction, adding up to nearly three seconds. Nobody intentionally queries the same table forty-seven times for one save. That count is the tell.

Here's the pattern that produces it: a business rule loops over every active incident, and for each one, opens a brand-new GlideRecord against the problem table and runs a fresh query to look up the linked problem record one at a time. Run this over fifty incidents, and the profiler doesn't show one problem query — it shows fifty.

Problem underscore id is already a reference field sitting on the incident record. Dot-walking it, writing incGr dot problem_id dot number, reads the related problem record through the reference ServiceNow already resolved, with no new GlideRecord object and no new query created on each pass through the loop. Same output, one query total, and the forty-seven repeated queries disappear from the profiler entirely.

The second repeating signature looks different: instead of many small repeated queries, it's one query that pulls far more data than anything uses — a full GlideRecord loop that fetches every matching incident just to increment a counter. GlideAggregate asks the database to do that counting and sends back only the number, turning a large, slow query into a small, fast one.

Once you can spot a repeated query or an oversized one in the profiler, the next pattern to recognize is a business rule that fires far more times than one user action should ever trigger. That's lesson seven: business rule loops and recursive triggers.
